# On Maps That Lie Kindly

Every useful map is a small, deliberate lie.

The London Underground map is the famous example. Harry Beck drew it in 1931 by ignoring geography almost entirely. Distances are wrong, rivers are smoothed away, and stations that are a ten-minute walk apart look like distant neighbors, while others that are far apart look close. The map is a diagram of connection, not a picture of the city. Passengers loved it immediately, because they didn't need to know where things *were*. They needed to know how to *get* there.

I find this a quietly profound point: the more faithfully a map reproduces the world, the less helpful it tends to be. Jorge Luis Borges and Lewis Carroll both imagined maps at a 1:1 scale, as big as the territory itself, and both understood the joke. Such a map would be perfectly accurate and perfectly useless. To understand anything, you have to decide what to leave out.

## Omission as a form of care

We usually treat simplification as a compromise, a regrettable loss of truth. But a good simplification is an act of respect for the person who will use it. A recipe doesn't tell you the molecular chemistry of the Maillard reaction. A road sign doesn't describe the town, only says *exit here*. A friend giving directions says, "Turn left at the ugly green house," which is useless to a satellite and perfect for you.

The skill is in choosing what to throw away. Throw away the wrong thing, like the one-way street or the cliff edge, and the map becomes dangerous. Throw away the right things, and a bewildering world suddenly becomes navigable.

## The trouble comes when we forget

The risk is that we start to mistake the map for the land. Our models of the world are mostly maps: economic indicators, personality types, diagnostic categories, résumés, the stories we tell about our own lives. Each one is helpful precisely because it's a simplification, and each becomes a trap when we forget that it is one.

A GDP figure doesn't tell you whether people are flourishing. A personality label doesn't tell you what someone will do on a hard day. A résumé is not a person. Even our memories are maps, redrawn every time we consult them, with the roads we prefer drawn a little wider.

## Holding a map well

Maybe the mature stance is neither to distrust maps nor to worship them, but to keep asking a few questions:

- **What was this made to help me do?** A subway map is great for riding trains and terrible for hiking.
- **What did the mapmaker leave out, and why?**
- **When did I last check it against the ground?**

The last question matters most. Every so often, you have to look up from the page and walk the actual streets, noticing the things no diagram would have told you: the smell of bread from a bakery that isn't marked, a shortcut through a courtyard, a view that stops you mid-step.

The best maps, I think, don't try to replace that experience. They get you to the right neighborhood, and then they quietly let you go.
